23654.etyen:
A merger of two historically distinct loanwords: one from Middle Low German hissen (“to urge on, incite”), also hessen and hitzen, from Middle High German hetzen (“to chase, pursue; drive on”), from Old High German hezzen (“to pursue”), from Proto-West Germanic *hattjan (“to hunt down, pursue”), from Proto-Germanic *hatjaną (“to hunt down, pursue; incite, attack”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱeh₂d- (“strong emotion”); and the other from German hitzen (“to heat, heat up”), from Middle High German hitzen (“to heat, become hot”), from Old High German hizzōn (“to glow, burn; become heate / Of uncertain immediate origin; compare Swedish hissa (“to hoist”). It belongs to a widespread nautical word family whose hoisting sense is attested in Middle Dutch hisen (“to hoist”) and Middle Low German hissen (“to hoist”). The deeper origin of the family is uncertain.
Compare Danish hisse and hejse, German hissen and Dutch hijsen (“to hoist”). Related borrowings include French hisser (“to hoist”), Italian issare (“to hoist”) and English hoist.

x: Vi reiste gjennom Bulgaria på vei til Svartehavet.
We travelled through Bulgaria on our way to the Black Sea.
Bulgaria er et land i det sørøstlige Europa.
Bulgaria is a country in southeastern Europe.

1000038.etyen:
Internationalism, based on Latin Bulgaria, a Medieval Latin formation from the ethnonym represented by Bulgarus (“Bulgar”) and -ia (“country-forming suffix”). The country is named after the Bulgars, a Turkic-speaking people who established the first Bulgarian state in the Balkans in the late seventh century.
The origin of the ethnonym is disputed. A widespread proposal derives it from Proto-Turkic *bulgar, from *bulga- (“to stir, mix”), perhaps originally meaning “mixed people” or “rebels”, but this interpretation is not universally accepted.
Compare Danish Bulgarien, Swedish Bulgarien, German

1000294.etyen: From French grave (“serious, low-pitched; back”), from Middle French grave, from Old French grave, from Latin gravis (“heavy, grave, serious”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷréh₂us (“heavy”), from *gʷreh₂- (“heavy”) + *-us (forms adjectives).

x: vi [badet] i det lunkne vannet og satt på knausene og månet oss, grasiøst innfiltret i hverandre
we [bathed] in the lukewarm water and sat on the rocky outcrops exposing ourselves to the moonlight, gracefully entangled with each other

1000806.etyen: From måne (“moon”), used as a denominal verb and formed after the model of sole (“to expose oneself to sunlight, sunbathe”). The reflexive måne seg is thus structurally parallel to å sole seg (“to sun oneself”), with moonlight rather than sunlight as that to which one exposes oneself.

1005158.etyen:
Compound of elefant (“elephant”) + hvitløk (“garlic”), literally “elephant garlic”.
The first element ultimately comes from Latin elephantus (“elephant”), from Ancient Greek ἐλέφᾱς (eléphās, “ivory; elephant”), of uncertain further origin. Within the second element, hvit (“white”) is from Old Norse hvítr (“white”), from Proto-Germanic *hwītaz (“white”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱweyt- (“to shine”); løk (“onion”) is from Old Norse laukr (“leek, onion, garlic”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *laukaz (“leek, onion”), of uncertain further origin.
